objective: Find the limiting oxygen index and map flammability boundaries of liquid fuels in microgravity.
experiment_type: Single droplet combustion, ISS (MDCA in CIR)
fuel_material: Methanol and n-heptane droplets, about 1.1 to 4.7 mm
environment: O2/N2 at about 0.7 to 1 atm, O2 mole fraction 0.12 to 0.34, ambient temperature 18 to 27 C, quiescent
variables_studied: O2 fraction, droplet size, pressure, fiber or free-floating, fuel
findings: Flames established in N2 at about 1 atm down to O2 of 0.12 (methanol) and 0.13 (heptane). K lower at lower oxygen in the Table IX tally. At O2 of 0.30 or more, 18 of 24 rows ended in disruption. S7 reports flaming at lower oxygen than in normal gravity.
safety_relevance: Liquid-fuel droplet flames persist at low oxygen in microgravity, relevant to atmosphere and suppression choices. Not applicable to solid materials without review.
evidence_level: Reported observation; trend summary is my tally
limitations: No LOI number stated in S1 main text. Fiber and free-floating pooled. Needle contamination affects some methanol and heptane disruption results. Droplets only.

objective: Quantify suppressant effectiveness of CO2 and find where quasi-steady burning stops.
experiment_type: Single droplet combustion with a diluent or suppressant gas
environment: O2/N2/CO2 at 1.0 atm (start 0.21 O2) and 0.70 atm (start 0.30 O2); CO2 up to 0.70; O2/N2/He tests numbered 226 to 280
variables_studied: CO2 or He fraction, O2 fraction, pressure, droplet size
findings: CO2 appears in 123 Table IX rows and He in 51. Example FLEX-140 (methanol, 0.15 O2/0.35 N2/0.50 CO2, 0.70 atm): extinction after 1.3 s, K 0.20 mm2/s. S7 reports K departing from quasi-steady predictions at very low O2 in high-CO2 ambient.
safety_relevance: CO2 is the ISS extinguishing gas, so results bear on suppressant effectiveness (S11).
limitations: Droplets only, two fuels. Exact CO2 suppression threshold not stated in the text read. Some tests ended early (droplet drift). Helium appears in Table IX but not in the S1 summary.

objective: Document how droplet flames extinguish across oxygen and diluent conditions.
findings: Radiative extinction at higher dilution with larger droplets; diffusive extinction at lower dilution with smaller droplets (S1). S7 reports radiative (not water-absorption) extinction below about 14% O2. Of 276 rows: 186 extinction, 62 disruption, 28 completion.
safety_relevance: Radiation, not convection, sets extinction limits for quiescent flames (S7).
limitations: S1 does not interpret its data. The 14% threshold is from S7 and approximate. Disruption may be influenced by needle contamination.

objective: Understand continued vaporization after the visible flame goes out.
fuel_material: n-heptane, large droplets (3.91, 3.48 and 2.49 mm cases at 1 atm)
environment: O2/N2 and O2/N2/CO2 at about 1 atm
variables_studied: Oxygen, CO2, droplet size, burning rate, extinction diameter
findings: After radiative extinction droplets kept vaporizing at a steady rate, then went out again at a finite diameter, with a vapor cloud near that point. Team hypothesis: low-temperature soot-free cool flame. Second-stage burning rate slightly lower.
safety_relevance: S7 suggests cool combustion persisting after hot-flame extinction may raise fire risk and possibly re-ignite. This is a hypothesis.
limitations: Second stage not visible in color or UV cameras. The 2012 journal paper was not read in full. Decane re-ignition claim has no data.

objective: Measure hot and cool stage burning rates and extinction diameters for three alkanes.
environment: O2/N2/CO2 and O2/He/N2 at 1.0, 0.7 and 0.5 atm, O2 14 to 25 percent
variables_studied: Oxygen, diluent, pressure, droplet size, K hot and cool, radiant power, extinction diameters
findings: All three alkanes showed hot-flame radiative extinction, cool-flame burning and a second extinction. Examples: decane R377 K 0.41 then 0.33; octane R298 K 0.48 then 0.38. Cool-flame extinction diameter scales roughly as O2 to the power -3/4 in O2/N2.
safety_relevance: Supports that cool-flame burning is general to n-alkanes.
evidence_level: Reported observation; scaling is preliminary theory
limitations: Many values only in plots. Droplets sometimes left view. Cross-diluent correlation scattered. Figure 1d caption composition inconsistent.

objective: Reproduce two-stage behavior and flow effects with a gaseous fuel source.
environment: Quiescent air and slow airflow (0 to 1 cm/s), zero gravity
findings: Hot flame extinguishes near 1200 K; cool flame near 700 K for about 18 s; flash re-ignition; about 3 mm/s airflow gives local extinction and about 0.4 Hz pulsation with no cool flame.
safety_relevance: Shows a possible mechanism for re-ignition, in simulation only.
limitations: Gas source, not a droplet. Optically thin radiation model. Not a measurement.

objective: Study structure and limits of non-premixed cool flames burning gaseous fuel.
experiment_type: Spherical non-premixed flames on a burner, ISS (CIR)
variables_studied: Thermal radiation, burner temperature, intensified-camera imaging
findings: June 2021 tests gave the first observation of spherical non-premixed cool flames burning gaseous fuel. Three cool flames were found in radiation and temperature data after hot flames were quenched. Intensified images showed the hot flame going out, about a second of darkness, then a much smaller cool flame.
safety_relevance: None stated. S2 ties the work to engine design and fuel ratings.
limitations: Press article with no numbers. Fuel and conditions not given. Cool flames too faint to see live.

objective: Test whether a cool flame near the droplet and a hot flame farther out can coexist.
variables_studied: Fuel leakage fraction, heat-of-combustion ratio (0.01 to 0.3), burning rate
findings: Dual flames possible only over a narrow range of conditions. Cited context: cool flames sit closer to the droplet (standoff ratio about 3) at about 780 K; for 50/50 decane/hexanol droplets at 0.05 to 0.3 MPa, hot-flame luminosity fell with pressure while broadband radiance stayed nearly constant and cool-flame radiant output rose to about half of the hot-flame level at 0.3 MPa.
evidence_level: Theory, with experimental context cited from other papers
limitations: One-step chemistry, thin flame sheets, unity Lewis number, no data comparison in the text. Experimental statements are cited, not shown.

objective: Study droplet-droplet interactions, fuel mixtures, surrogate fuels, soot formation and weak convective flow.
fuel_material: Iso-octane (one documented test point). Planned: n-decane, ethanol, heptane-hexadecane, propanol-glycerol, decane-propylbenzene, n-heptane-toluene, propylbenzene, toluene
environment: Not stated in the sources read
variables_studied: Burning rate and manner, soot formation conditions, mixture evaporation
findings: A ground-commanded iso-octane test point ran on July 2, 2014 (S8). No measured results in the sources read.
limitations: No data. S8 does not say the iso-octane test used a mixture.

objective: FLEX-2J: flame spread and droplet motion along a droplet array. ICE-GA: ignition and combustion of surrogate biofuels.
fuel_material: FLEX-2J n-heptane. ICE-GA 50-50 n-heptane/ethanol and 50-50 n-hexanol/n-decane
environment: Planned. FLEX-2J droplets about 1 mm, spacing ratios 4 to 14 (to be determined in S7)
variables_studied: Droplet spacing, pressure, gas composition, burning rate, flame spread
findings: No results. S9 (May 2015) shows hardware prepared and a first FLEX-2J test planned for early June 2015, with a linear droplet array of fixed and free droplets.
limitations: S7 plans changed (timing slipped to 2015). ICE-GA has no update. No results.

objective: Study how fuel thickness affects flame spread and extinction
environment: BASS-II small flow duct in the Microgravity Science Glovebox; forced opposed airflow; low oxygen and low flow conditions (exact values are test-specific)
variables_studied: film thickness; airflow speed; oxygen concentration
findings: The work package examined how fuel thickness affects flame spread and extinction; no single extinction velocity is assigned to all PMMA films
safety_relevance: Thin polymer films may behave differently from thicker parts; record thickness; orientation; ventilation and oxygen when screening materials
limitations: Condition-specific; distinct from the 1-5 mm flat-sample series; exact conditions must be copied from the test matrix
geometry: Thin film (about 0.1-0.4 mm thick; 1 or 2 cm wide)

objective: Compare flame spread across thickness and flow settings
environment: BASS-II flow duct inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox; opposed airflow of about 3-20 cm/s; oxygen varied per test
variables_studied: sample thickness (1-5 mm); width (1 or 2 cm); one-sided or two-sided burning; airflow speed; oxygen concentration
findings: Flame position over time was tracked to calculate spread rate; the series supports comparison across thickness and flow settings
safety_relevance: A thicker polymer part may have different heat feedback and flame spread from a thin film; record exact thickness and flow
limitations: Not to be mixed with thin-film data; oxygen must be attached to each test ID
geometry: Flat sample (1-5 mm thick; 1 or 2 cm wide)

objective: Measure flame spread and extinction behaviour over rod-shaped PMMA
experiment_type: Solid fuel flame spread and extinction (microgravity)
environment: BASS-II duct; opposed flow; hot wire ignition near the downstream end; oxygen and flow vary by rod diameter (see Table 4.2)
variables_studied: rod diameter (6.35; 9.525; 12.7 mm); oxygen concentration; flow velocity; black or clear PMMA
findings: Flame spread and extinction behaviour over rods was measured; the report distinguishes diameters and black or clear samples; clear-PMMA data are limited
safety_relevance: Component shape and diameter can influence flame spread and extinction; rod results cannot be directly transferred to sheets or fabrics
limitations: Check the specific Table 4.2 row before quoting any value

objective: Test flame behaviour of a cotton-fiberglass fabric under varied oxygen and flow
environment: BASS-II flow duct; concurrent flow; oxygen and flow speed varied (Table 7.1)
variables_studied: sample width (1.2 or 2.2 cm); concurrent flow speed; oxygen concentration
findings: Outcomes recorded per test include quenched; no ignition; blow-off and no blow-off; example GMT45-T4 (2.2 cm; flow 10 to 2.2 cm/s; O2 18.7 vol%) quenched and GMT190-T21 (1.2 cm; flow 11 to 47 cm/s; O2 17.2 vol%) blow-off
safety_relevance: The cotton fraction is combustible while the fiberglass mesh keeps the sample structure; results are condition-specific
limitations: Test-specific; not universal thresholds; the report notes some O2 readings may be inaccurate
geometry: Fabric (about 0.32 mm thick; area density 18.2 mg/cm2)

experiment_name: Burning Rate Emulator (gaseous-fuel emulation of condensed fuels)
objective: Study material flammability and extinction using gaseous fuels that emulate condensed fuels
fuel_material: Gaseous fuels (including inert-gas mixtures) emulating paper; plastic and alcohol
environment: Combustion Integrated Rack; flat porous burner; burner heat flux and surface temperature used to control fuel flow
variables_studied: fuel mixture and flow rate; burner heat flux; burner surface temperature; flame size; surrounding atmosphere
findings: NASA reports analysis of 59 BRE burn tests covering heat flow; flame size and fuel-mixture flow effects; the public summary has no material-by-material table
safety_relevance: Can support screening of materials and flammability test methods in low and partial gravity; it is not proof that a named material is safe
limitations: Emulation method; not a direct burn test of named materials; not all parameters were measured in every run
evidence_location: NASA Science BRE page and NASA article Studying Combustion and Fire Safety
